26 MB at idle.

decline is a terminal for macOS, and it gets through a cat of 100 MB in 0.58 s. Here it is next to Ghostty and kitty, on the same Mac on 2 November.

2 November 2026, medians of 5 runs.
MeasuredeclineGhosttykitty
Idle memory26 MB60 MB99 MB
Four tabs47 MB87 MB104 MB
cat of 100 MB0.58 s0.66 s1.05 s
cat CPU, with WindowServer0.66 s2.04 s1.63 s
Idle CPU0.02%0.03%0.12%

Apple M1 Max, macOS 27.0. decline at 7849ad4 (cat and idle CPU at 82c455f), Ghostty 1.4.0, kitty 0.49.2. Menlo 13, 100×30 cells, 10k lines of scrollback, one window. Memory is physical footprint across all of a terminal's processes. Runs taken in turns on a Mac with other work going on (load 3 to 6). The script

These runs did not compare input latency. decline doesn't always win either: in a separate run on 30 October, Ghostty's cat took 0.53 s to decline's 0.61 s. That run has its own write-up.

Apple Silicon, macOS 14 Sonoma or later, MIT licence. Install with Homebrew or read the source.

A terminal your agent can use without opening a window

decline ctl runs a program in a real terminal with no window, so an agent or a test can type into it, wait on it and read the screen back.

decline ctl spawn --name man --size 100x30 -- man ls

decline ctl wait-for man --text SYNOPSIS --timeout 5000

decline ctl screenshot man man.png

decline ctl kill man

Read the cells as well as the text

screen prints what's on screen as text. screen --json adds every cell's character, colours and attributes, plus the cursor, the title, the terminal's modes and whether the alternate screen is up.

So a test can check more than whether a word appeared. It can check that the word is bold, that the right row is highlighted, or that vim really did leave the alternate screen.

decline ctl screen man --json

Captured: three pieces of the 145 KB reply from that same session.

"alt_screen":true

"cursor":{"blink":false,"col":1,"row":29,"shape":"block","visible":true}

{"bg":"#16181c","bold":true,"fg":"#d8dee9","t":"N","x":0}

Know when a command has finished

Scraping a prompt to guess whether make test is done works until it doesn't. Start a session with spawn --shell, type with send, and wait-for --command comes back when the command ends, with its exit status, how long it took and the command itself.

Here ls failed with status 1 after 2,021 ms. (The sleep 2 is there to give it something to wait for.)

decline ctl spawn --name sh --shell

decline ctl send sh --text 'sleep 2; ls /nonexistent' --key enter

decline ctl wait-for sh --command --timeout 10000

Captured reply:

{"command":"sleep 2; ls /nonexistent","duration_ms":2021,"elapsed_ms":1991,"matched":true,"ok":true,"reason":"command","status":1}

Replace the sleep in your script

wait-for blocks until text shows up, a regex matches, the output goes quiet or the program exits. It exits 0 on a match, 3 when the timeout came first and 5 when the program quit without ever showing the text, so a script can tell those apart.

send goes through the app's own key encoding, kitty keyboard protocol included, so ctrl+c in a session reaches the program as ctrl+c.

decline ctl wait-for vim --idle 500

decline ctl wait-for vim --exit

decline ctl send top --key ctrl+c --text q

Watch it when you want to

Add --window and the session is a real window of the app, opened in the background without taking focus. Every ctl command works on it, and closing the window ends the session.

A session nothing has asked about for 30 minutes is killed, so forgotten tests don't keep a server running. decline has no assistant of its own and no account. ctl is for the agent you already use.

decline ctl spawn --window --name vim --size 100x30 -- vim

decline ctl kill vim

When you're the one typing

Under ctl is a terminal you can use yourself, written in Rust and drawn with Metal, with native Mac tabs and split panes. Press Tab and zsh's matches come up in a list, with what each flag does taken from its man page or --help.

Completion as you type, coloured output and copy on select are there if you want them, and off until you do.

decline settings

The settings screen, in any terminal.

decline import ghostty

Your Ghostty config, turned into decline's.

A program as its own app

decline pin rush --dock makes ~/Applications/rush.app and puts it in the Dock. Clicking it opens a window running rush and nothing else, with its own icon and settings. You'll need rush installed. Any other command works the same way.

If the program ships an icon, the pin uses it. Otherwise decline draws one: the initial over the Slope, on one of ten fixed colours hashed from the name, so the same name always gets the same pin.

decline pin Rush --icon rush.png --cwd ~/code -- rush

decline pin --list

decline pin --edit rush

decline pin --remove rush

Installing it

brew install --cask 0xdeafcafe/tap/terminal-decline

That's Terminal Decline.app, plus the command as both terminal-decline and decline. You'll need an Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 14 Sonoma or later.

The in-app updater is built, but there are no signed and notarised releases for it to offer yet.

  • Source on GitHub
  • The README, with the whole feature list
  • The ctl docs
  • The changelog
  • The MIT licence

git clone https://github.com/0xdeafcafe/terminal-decline

cd terminal-decline

scripts/dogfood.sh --open

From source, as the app. You'll need Rust and the Xcode command line tools.

cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/0xdeafcafe/terminal-decline terminal-decline

From source, as the bare command. No app bundle, so no Dock pins made from the app and no updater.
